title: Cache Placement Policies
summary: Direct-mapped, fully associative, and set-associative placement — where a memory block is allowed to live in the cache.

slides.subTitle: Where can a block go?
slides.markdown:
A cache is far smaller than RAM, so many memory blocks must share the same small set of cache slots. **Placement policy** decides: given a block's address, which slot(s) in the cache is it allowed to occupy?

This single design decision drives a direct trade-off between hardware cost and how well the cache avoids unnecessary evictions — the three schemes below sit at different points on that trade-off.

slides.subTitle: One possible slot
slides.markdown:
In a **direct-mapped** cache, each memory block maps to exactly **one** possible cache slot, computed directly from its address (typically `address mod number_of_slots`). Checking for a hit means looking at one slot and comparing one tag.

This is the cheapest and fastest hardware to build, but it's also the most prone to **conflict misses**: two frequently-used blocks that happen to map to the same slot will keep evicting each other, even if the rest of the cache sits idle.

slides.subTitle: Any slot, at a cost
slides.markdown:
In a **fully associative** cache, a block can go in **any** slot at all. This eliminates conflict misses entirely — a block only gets evicted when the whole cache is genuinely full, never because of an unlucky address collision.

The cost is hardware: every lookup must compare the requested tag against *every* slot's tag in parallel, which needs a comparator per slot. That scales badly, which is why fully associative designs are reserved for small structures (like TLBs), not large L1/L2/L3 caches.

slides.subTitle: The practical middle ground
slides.markdown:
A **set-associative** cache splits slots into **sets**, each holding **N** ways (lines). A block's address picks exactly one set (like direct-mapped), but within that set it can occupy any of the N ways (like fully associative on a small scale).

This is what essentially every real L1/L2/L3 cache uses — commonly 4-way, 8-way, or 16-way — because it captures most of fully associative's conflict-avoidance benefit while needing only N comparators per set instead of one per entire cache.

slides.subTitle: Tag, index, offset
slides.markdown:
Every cache access splits the address into three fields.

![An address split into tag, index, and offset bits](assets/tag-index-offset.svg)

**Offset** picks the byte within a line; **index** picks the set (skipped entirely in fully associative caches); **tag** is compared against the way(s) in that set to confirm a hit. More ways per set means fewer index bits and more tag bits — the hardware trade-off behind associativity.

assets.alt: An address split into tag, index, and offset bits

slides.subTitle: A worked example
slides.markdown:
```text
Cache: 64 sets, 64-byte lines -> 6 offset bits, 6 index bits
Address: 0x00001A40  (binary tag|index|offset split below)

Direct-mapped (1 way, 64 sets):
  index = (address / 64) mod 64

4-way set-associative (16 sets, 4 ways):
  index = (address / 64) mod 16   <- fewer index bits, more tag bits
  tag   = remaining upper bits; compared against all 4 ways in that set
```

Going from 1-way to 4-way at the same total capacity means 4x fewer sets, so the index shrinks by 2 bits and the tag grows by 2 bits — more comparison hardware, fewer conflict-prone sets.

slides.subTitle: Hit rate vs hardware cost
slides.markdown:
| Scheme | Conflict misses | Comparators needed | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct-mapped | Most | 1 per slot | Very large, latency-critical structures |
| Set-associative (N-way) | Few | N per set | Nearly all real L1/L2/L3 caches |
| Fully associative | None | 1 per every slot | Small structures (TLBs, victim caches) |

**How to decide:** as capacity grows, full associativity's per-slot comparator cost becomes prohibitive — that's why large caches settle on set-associative (4- to 16-way) as the practical sweet spot between direct-mapped's conflicts and fully associative's hardware bill.
